segments.title: Objectives versus annihilation in a fictional space battle
segments.summary: A capture-point battle shows how positional victory, enemy destruction, and accumulated damage can pull a commander toward different definitions of success.
segments.body: Battlefleet Gothic: Armada II makes the choice between mission objectives and enemy destruction visible. The fleet spreads out to seize several strategic areas before concentrating combat power against the opposing vessel. Holding space continues to earn victory points while the enemy survives, so the operational objective can decide the engagement before annihilation. The playthrough nevertheless pursues the opponent, revealing the appeal of a more decisive-looking result than the mission requires. Damage carried out of the battle also affects later operations, giving tactical aggression a continuing cost. This fictional example is useful for studying mission focus, positional control, and the difference between winning an engagement and eliminating the opposing force.

evidence.note: The game explains that victory need not require engaging the enemy, while Clarke instead plans to provoke combat and divide ships between capture points.
He captures multiple strategic areas, fights the opposing ship, and then notes that battles leave damage which must be considered afterward.

segments.title: Building the economy before expanding the fleet
segments.summary: The tutorial demands new military spending, while the campaign prioritises productive worlds and selective defences to avoid another bankruptcy.
segments.body: After the first victory, the tutorial pushes the purchase of ships, mines, and defences. The previous campaign went bankrupt after following these demands, and minefields have little value where no counterattack is expected. Scarce funds instead go into worlds that generate continuing income. This turns the campaign economy into a force-planning problem: immediate military purchases compete with investment in the revenue base that sustains later operations. A defensive platform is still funded at an important location because that expenditure has a plausible operational payoff. The fictional system offers a clear example of opportunity cost, threat-based defence spending, and the danger of expanding a fleet faster than its economy can support.

evidence.note: Clarke identifies tutorial-directed ship and mine purchases as the cause of his earlier bankruptcy and argues that defenses without an expected counterattack waste scarce funds.
He upgrades economic worlds, selectively adds a platform to an important location, and waits for the improved worlds to produce income.

segments.title: Fleet composition and the value of a cruiser reserve
segments.summary: Pre-battle reorganisation compares cruisers with frigates under a deployment limit and shows why an extra cruiser can be more useful than several escorts.
segments.body: As campaign income improves, the fleets are rebuilt according to their needs instead of buying ships indiscriminately. Available cruiser statistics are compared, escorts are added where formations need them, and the final force must fit a fixed deployment allowance. One formation fields three cruisers and four frigates while another cruiser waits to provide support. That choice separates hull count from the combat weight and resilience of larger ships. A reserve cruiser can reinforce a damaged formation instead of entering automatically at the start. The classes and numbers belong to a science-fiction game, but the decision introduces force mix, deployment constraints, and reinforcement planning.

evidence.note: Clarke plans repairs and purchases, compares cruiser values, and selects a Dauntless-class cruiser for one fleet.
He works within the deployment total, describes a force of cruisers and frigates, and values an additional cruiser that can arrive in support if damage is suffered.

segments.title: Target priorities and attacks on enemy mobility
segments.summary: Smaller enemy ships are attacked before the larger vessel, engines become the priority subsystem, and positional scoring remains tied to the tactical fight.
segments.body: This fictional engagement turns target selection into a visible command problem. The attack begins against the smaller enemy ships, then shifts to the larger vessel with its engines marked as the priority subsystem. Disabling propulsion limits the opponent's ability to manoeuvre or escape. Meanwhile, the attacking force occupies strategic areas and builds a points lead, so ship attacks support the mission objective. When the opponent tries to neutralise one area, pressure stays on the last ship instead of sending every vessel away to recapture it. Boarding and lightning strikes finish the target, and the game awards an overwhelming victory. The sequence illustrates target order, attacks on mobility, and the balance between tactical destruction and positional scoring.

evidence.note: Clarke reports that the rebuilt economy is supporting the fleet, then orders the smaller enemy ships attacked first and makes the larger ship's engines the priority target.
His force accumulates strategic points, contests an area, cripples the remaining enemy through boarding attacks, and receives an overwhelming-victory result.

segments.title: Avoiding fixed defenses and timing the escort attack
segments.summary: The fleet bypasses a fortified position, uses stealth and observation to locate the enemy, then waits until hostile fighters are gone before sending escorts into torpedo range.
segments.body: The assault keeps the fleet away from fixed defences rather than attacking their strongest point directly. Silent running and observation of enemy fighter movement help clarify the tactical picture before the main commitment. The game also makes maximum burn a tradeoff because a ship cannot stop promptly after using it. Once hostile fighters can no longer threaten the smaller ships, the escorts accelerate into torpedo range. Their timing becomes part of a combined action: capital ships absorb attention and remove threats, then lighter vessels exploit the safer approach. Boarding attacks and long-range weapons further divide the enemy's defensive problem. As a fictional example, the battle explains reconnaissance, bypassing fortifications, escort protection, and deliberate sequencing of combat capabilities.

evidence.note: The fleet uses silent running, avoids the defense platforms, observes enemy fighters, and learns the movement penalty attached to maximum burn.
Clarke delays attacking the defenses, then explains that the escorts can rush forward once there is nothing left for them to defend against and can reach torpedo range sooner.

segments.title: Strategic geography guides the next campaign objective
segments.summary: Comparing a heavily defended hive world with a food-producing agricultural world shows how value, enemy strength, and logistical benefit shape campaign priorities.
segments.body: Between battles, nearby objectives are compared by value and risk rather than distance alone. A cardinal hive world has a fleet too strong to fight immediately, while an agricultural world offers food and appears attainable. The chosen objective therefore reflects both productive value and the force required to capture it. In the next deployment, small enemy ships begin directly on capture points and create an early positional advantage. Point-seizing vessels and the main combat force receive separate tasks in response. The geography and resources are fictional, but the decision illustrates intelligence assessment, logistical objectives, and matching ambition to available strength.

evidence.note: Clarke compares enemy fleet strength at a hive world with the food value and accessibility of an agricultural world.
He allocates ships to capture points, notes the enemy's forward deployment, and identifies destruction of the opposing fleet as another route to success.

segments.title: Concentrating ships by coordinating arrival times
segments.summary: Ship groups receive different speed orders so the lighter units reach the enemy with support, followed by a decision to mass the fleet on one capture point.
segments.body: Two groups are released to hunt, then their speeds are adjusted so they reach the enemy at roughly the same time. Without that correction, the faster ships would arrive first and face the fight alone. The fictional battle therefore demonstrates concentration in time, where coordinated arrival matters alongside the number of ships assigned. The whole fleet then masses on one strategic area to take it from the opponent and widen an existing points lead. Victory arrives before every remaining objective is captured. The result reinforces the difference between sufficient operational success and complete occupation.

evidence.note: Clarke assigns hunting missions and changes speeds so separate ship groups arrive together rather than exposing the faster group alone.
He concentrates the entire fleet on one strategic area, extends the points advantage, and wins before clearing every remaining objective.

segments.title: Fast frigates and stealthy cruisers divide the mission
segments.summary: Cruisers approach under stealth while two frigates sprint toward capture areas, allowing combat and positional tasks to proceed at the same time.
segments.body: Different ship types receive different movement orders before contact. The cruisers approach under stealth while two frigates sprint toward capture areas, using the smaller ships' speed without placing them at the head of the main attack. Three opposing cruisers appear along the route, yet the division of labour lets strategic areas change hands while the heavier ships fight. Boarding, lightning strikes, and gunnery contribute to victory alongside the rising point total. The sequence depicts fictional game mechanics. It still provides a useful example of task organisation, scouting uncertainty, and assigning light units to positional work.

evidence.note: Clarke gives the cruiser groups stealth orders, sends two frigates ahead at speed, and then identifies roughly three enemy cruisers on their route.
The fleet captures several strategic areas while fighting the enemy cruisers, accumulates points alongside the combat, and reaches victory.

segments.title: Budget-limited fleet expansion and local defense
segments.summary: The campaign unlocks another fleet before the economy can afford it, so existing ships, repairs, and local fortifications answer the enemy incursion.
segments.body: The game authorises another fleet before the campaign can afford one. Existing force strength, available points, and the relative value of candidate ships determine what the current budget can support. When an enemy incursion appears, two fleets move toward the threatened system and local fortifications are added where funds allow. A stronger defensive option remains unavailable because the treasury lacks the required money. Procurement, maintenance, and fixed defence therefore compete inside the same campaign economy. The fictional setting makes the difference between authorised and affordable force structure easy to see, along with the role of local defences in supporting mobile forces.

evidence.note: The campaign unlocks a new fleet, but Clarke says he lacks the money, compares current fleet values, and selects ships within the available points.
An enemy incursion prompts fleet movements and defensive construction, while a stronger fortification remains unaffordable.
